column3: It rejects worship besides God and commands worship of Him alone as the upright religion.
The affirmation of messengerhood only broadly supports the proclamation context.
Courtly nearness is a political reward, contrasting with the claimed nearness to God through intermediaries.
It directly addresses taking protectors besides God and reasserts God's sole guardianship.
The preceding verse explicitly commands worshiping God with religion made sincere for Him.
Its reform, reliance, and return to God offer only a general monotheistic parallel.
God judges religious disagreement and guides believers to truth, developing the focus's judgment clause.
It repeats the command to worship God with religion made sincere for Him.
The speaker declares worship of God alone with personal religious sincerity.
God's final judgment of disputes after knowing truth parallels the focus's judgment between rival claims.
The devotional virtues are compatible with sincere religion but do not address intermediaries or judgment.
God's mastery of the Day of Religion supports the focus's final divine judgment.
It explicitly says the Lord will decide the matters over which people differed.
Its declaration that God is the One, the Subduer reinforces the exclusive divine status at issue.
Pharaoh's charge of ingratitude shows how disbelief can be rhetorically recast as disloyalty.
It invokes God as the judge between servants concerning their disagreements.
It condemns worship besides God and identifies its final loss.
The warning to disbelievers is a broad consequence parallel without the intermediary claim.
It denies that wealth or children bring people near to God and defines true nearness by faith and good deeds.
It argues for direct worship of the Creator to whom all return.
Following rightly guided messengers without payment is only a secondary proclamation parallel.
It directly contrasts protectors taken besides God with God as the real Protector.
God's true creation and ordered rule reinforce the exclusive sovereignty presupposed by the focus.
Human creation from a drop does not clarify sincere religion, intermediaries, or judgment.
God will judge competing religious communities over their disagreements.
God's power over souls is nearby context but does not develop the focus's worship claim.
Promised nearness in Pharaoh's court provides a contrasting worldly use of the nearness motif.
Religious pretense and division offer a distant parallel to false worship claims.
It states that truth has come while many hate it, supporting the focus's exposure of false claims.
The woe to deniers is a generic warning without a specific link to the focus's argument.
It prohibits treating mockers of religion as protectors, relevant to corrupted religious allegiance.
God's sole lordship and the declaration of no god but Him reinforce exclusive devotion.
The repeated woe to deniers adds only a general consequence of disbelief.
It contrasts God, who guides to truth, with partners who cannot guide unless guided.
The punishment warning is nearby but does not specify false intermediaries or sincere religion.
The drawing near of Pharaoh's party in the sea narrative has no material relation to the focus.
It connects God's revealed Book, judgment by it, and disbelief in rejecting that judgment.
Truthful revelation and believing it reinforce the focus's contrast between truth and falsehood.
The commercial documentation rule does not clarify worship, nearness, or religious judgment.
It rejects protectors besides God as powerless and declares Him the One, the Subduer.
The barrier before disbelievers is not an explanatory parallel to the focus.
Those who take devils as protectors besides God wrongly assume themselves guided.
It denies efficacy to those invoked besides God, directly undermining intermediary worship.
It states that God does not approve disbelief and that all return to Him for disclosure.
Security for faith unmingled with wrongdoing does not develop the focus's specific claim.
God's not guiding those left astray parallels the focus's denial of guidance to the lying disbeliever.
Joseph's low sale price does not clarify the focus's religious argument.
It links established religion with worshiping God alone and associating nothing with Him.
God will make disputed truth clear and expose disbelievers as liars.
The chronological dispute about Abraham does not materially illuminate the focus.
The question about being held to account invokes the Day of Religion central to final judgment.
It assigns all rule on that Day to God, who judges between people.
Earlier deniers receiving unforeseen punishment reinforce the focus's warning against disbelief.
Their disbelief in the message followed by future knowing parallels rejection and eventual exposure.
It challenges the taking of gods besides God and their supposed power over resurrection.
The marital exception does not bear on the focus's theological claims.
It identifies the great news as the matter over which people differ, echoing the focus's dispute clause.
God's guidance to a straight path is a broad contrast to the focus's denial of guidance.
The command to be among the first submitters continues the local call to exclusive obedience.
It identifies denial of the Day of Religion, supporting the focus's judgment horizon.
Denying God's signs and turning away brings punishment but does not address intermediary worship.
It names God as the true Lord and all that follows truth's rejection as misguidance.
Turning away and disbelieving supplies the moral category named at the focus's close.
The mutual alliance obligations of believers do not clarify taking protectors besides God.
It directly rejects taking intercessors besides God on the ground that they possess nothing.
The question about the Day of Religion invokes the future judgment denied by disbelievers.
It commands calling on the living God with religion made sincere for Him.
It contrasts alleged partners with God as the sole originator and renewer of creation.
The woe for disbelievers on their promised Day is a general judgment parallel.
The condemnation of an ungrateful sinner is only a broad moral parallel to disbelief.
It warns that associating partners with God voids deeds, directly excluding mixed worship.
The emphatic denial of signs is a general disbelief parallel without the focus's mechanism.
People call on God with sincere religion in peril, then associate partners after rescue.
God's exclusive dominion, life-giving, and death-dealing support His sole divine authority.
The vision on the clear horizon does not clarify the focus's theological contrast.
It commands judgment by what God revealed and calls refusal of that judgment rebellious.
It declares that all intercession belongs to God, directly answering the intermediary rationale.
Its description of Jesus as among those brought near distinguishes granted nearness from claimed mediation.
God's judgment between parties is present, but the legal migration setting is remote from the focus.
The parable of many contending masters versus one master vividly explains undivided devotion.
Fabricating lies about God and denying His signs matches the focus's liar-disbeliever diagnosis.
Humanity's pronounced ingratitude provides a moral parallel to the focus's disbelief.
The reward of the excellent does not clarify the focus's critique of intermediary worship.
It identifies the truly brought-near, contrasting God-given nearness with an alleged route through idols.
The warning that people will know who receives humiliating punishment exposes lying claims.
Forgiveness and reward for the righteous are nearby but not a specific development of the focus.
Entering the Fire on the Day of Religion develops the final consequence of disbelief.
Inheritance and contractual entitlement do not bear on the focus's argument.
The fate of the arrogant disbelievers supplies the local outcome of refusing God's exclusive claim.
It sharply separates rival religions, clarifying that religious allegiance cannot be shared.
The believer contrasts truthful evidence for God with a liar and warns of the promised consequence.
It calls Satan ungrateful to his Lord, providing a pointed model of kufr toward God.
It links disbelief with harmful practices that divide people, a remote contrast to pure religion.
Assigning a portion of God's servants to Him is condemned as manifest human ingratitude.
The description of hostile disbelievers at the sanctuary does not clarify the focus's theological claim.
The frowning incident has no material relation to sincere religion or intermediaries.
The Quran benefits believers but increases wrongdoers in loss, supporting the focus's truth-disbelief divide.
God's prior word delays the judgment that will settle the matters over which people differ.
A dispute around the sleepers confirms God's promise but only distantly parallels the focus's disagreement.
It places the two sides under the alternative of clear guidance or clear error while affirming God as provider.
It describes people who take equals besides God and love them as they should love God, directly exposing divided devotion.
It calls for worship of God alone, no association with Him, and no taking one another as lords besides God.
It identifies associating partners with God as the decisive unpardoned theological offense.
It repeats the warning that association with God is a grave departure from the true path.
It rejects making the Messiah divine and commands worship of God as the Lord of all.
It condemns claims that divide or multiply God's divinity and affirms one God.
The final gathering asks alleged partners to account for the claims made about them.
The messenger is forbidden to worship those called on besides God and commanded to follow revelation.
It condemns inventing partners for God and falsely attributing offspring to Him.
It depicts a ritual division of offerings between God and alleged partners, illustrating compromised devotion.
Those who associate partners invoke God's will to defend their false practice, a related lying claim.
Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are declared wholly for God alone.
It explicitly denies that God has any partner and grounds submission in that exclusivity.
It challenges partners that create nothing and cannot help themselves or their worshipers.
It condemns taking religious authorities as lords besides God despite the command to worship one God.
It directly reports worship of powerless beings besides God as alleged intercessors with Him.
At final gathering, alleged partners disown their worshipers and the association between them collapses.
It rejects the supposed reality of those whom people call God's partners and exposes reliance on conjecture.
It challenges the naming of partners for God, who knows and sustains every soul.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created.
Associators appeal to divine will to excuse worship besides God, a parallel false rationale.
It prohibits setting another god beside God and states the resulting blame and abandonment.
It calls alleged beings besides God unable to remove harm or alter it.
Those invoked besides God themselves seek nearness to their Lord, directly overturning their use as routes to nearness.
It rejects taking gods besides God without clear authority for doing so.
It describes taking gods besides God in the hope that they will provide honor.
It argues that multiple gods would corrupt the heavens and earth, affirming God's singular transcendence.
It rebukes worship of things besides God that neither benefit nor harm.
It condemns calling on besides God what neither harms nor benefits as manifest error.
It identifies God as the True and all invoked besides Him as false.
It condemns calling on another god alongside God without proof and assigns such persons their reckoning with Him.
It rejects gods taken besides God that create nothing and cannot control death, life, or resurrection.
Taking one's own desire as a god supplies a related model of false religious allegiance.
It repeatedly contrasts God's creative acts with the claim that another god exists beside Him.
It calls the objects worshiped besides God idols that cannot provide, and commands seeking provision from God alone.
Even the associators acknowledge God as creator, exposing the inconsistency of their rival worship.
Alleged partners provide no intercession and their worshipers ultimately disbelieve in them.
It asks whether any alleged partner shares God's acts of creation, provision, death, and life.
It names association with God as a tremendous wrong.
Those called besides God possess not even the smallest independent power in heaven or earth.
It restricts intercession to God's permission, correcting the claimed authority of intermediaries.
It asks whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth, affirming exclusive deity.
God's cosmic sovereignty contrasts with invoked beings that possess no share even of a date stone.
It rejects taking gods besides the Merciful because their intercession cannot avail and they cannot save.
It records the arrogant refusal to affirm that there is no god but God.
In distress people call on God sincerely, then assign rivals to Him after relief.
Those who admit God created all are challenged over the incapacity of beings invoked besides Him.
It contrasts aversion at mention of God alone with joy at mention of those besides Him.
It rebukes any command to worship other than God despite clear knowledge.
It commands worship of God and gratitude, supplying the positive alternative to divided worship.
It states that people disbelieved when God alone was invoked but believed when partners were associated with Him.
It contrasts the call to God without partner with the call to the Fire through association.
It challenges partners who legislate a religion God has not authorized.
It denies independent intercession to those called besides God, except under God's truth and knowledge.
It challenges those called besides God to show any created share or warrant for their worship.
It calls no one more astray than those who invoke besides God beings unable to answer them.
The named goddesses are a concrete instance of the rival cults challenged by the focus.
It commands that no one be invoked alongside God in places of worship.
The messenger declares that he calls only on his Lord and associates no one with Him.
It explicitly commands worshiping God with religion made sincere for Him, prayer, and almsgiving.
